docs.text: Automated Pork Packaging Inspection Project Overview This project investigates automated detection of pork rasher packaging defects and visual meat presentation errors using computer vision. The project compares two computational approaches: Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) with Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification. YOLO11n deep-learning object detection. Inspection Categories The system evaluates five defect categories: Loose meat Packaging error Twisted meat Unsealed packaging Wrinkle These categories relate to packaging quality and visible meat presentation. The system does not evaluate freshness or food safety. Main Findings The extended YOLO11n model achieved the following performance on the held-out test dataset: Metric Result Precision 47.44% Recall 51.64% mAP@0.5 55.80% mAP@0.5:0.95 25.50% Although YOLO outperformed the HOG + SVM baseline during validation, missed defects and reduced test performance indicate that further improvements are required before industrial deployment. docs.text: Dataset Preparation 1. Dataset Overview The project uses RGB images of pork rasher products with bounding-box annotations for packaging and visual meat presentation defects. The original dataset was exported in COCO JSON format and contains five annotated defect categories: COCO ID Defect Category 1 Loose meat 2 Packaging error 3 Twisted meat 4 Unsealed 5 Wrinkle COCO category ID 0 is an unused placeholder and is excluded from the YOLO class mapping. 2. Original Dataset The original dataset contains 1,955 images and 2,466 bounding-box annotations. Dataset Images Annotations Training 1,764 2,232 Validation 115 143 Testing 76 91 Total 1,955 2,466 Images and annotations were inspected using Python, OpenCV, pandas and Matplotlib. 3. Dataset Quality Checks The dataset exploration included: Counting images and annotations in each split. Examining class distributions. Displaying images with ground-truth bounding boxes. Checking for invalid annotation geometry. Identifying duplicated original filenames across splits. No invalid bounding boxes were identified by the implemented geometry checks. However, original-image filename overlaps were identified between training, validation and testing datasets. Such overlaps can cause data leakage and produce overly optimistic evaluation results. 4. Duplicate Handling Images were grouped by their original source filename. Each original-image group was assigned to only one dataset split using the following priority: Test Validation Training This approach prevents copies with the same original filename from appearing across different splits. For validation and testing, one exported copy per original image was retained. Training copies were preserved. The resulting dataset was saved separately under data/processed/ to avoid modifying the original files. 5. Processed Dataset Dataset Images Annotations Training 1,741 2,201 Validation 114 144 Testing 76 93 Total 1,931 2,438 The processed dataset was verified by checking: Existence of all referenced image files. Valid image and category references. Positive bounding-box dimensions. Bounding boxes within image boundaries. No cross-split original-filename overlaps. All implemented validation checks passed. 6. COCO-to-YOLO Conversion The processed COCO annotations were converted to YOLO format for object-detection training. COCO bounding boxes use: [x_min, y_min, width, height] YOLO labels use: [class_id, x_center, y_center, width, height] The YOLO box coordinates are normalised by the corresponding image width and height. The five classes were mapped to consecutive YOLO IDs: YOLO ID Defect Category 0 Loose meat 1 Packaging error 2 Twisted meat 3 Unsealed 4 Wrinkle Each image has a corresponding text label file. Images without annotations have empty label files. The converted dataset is stored under data/yolo/ . 7. Dataset Limitations Class Imbalance The dataset contains unequal numbers of examples across defect categories. This may reduce detection performance for less-represented classes. Wrinkle Category The processed training set contains wrinkle annotations, but the validation and test datasets contain none. Therefore, the model's ability to detect wrinkle defects cannot be reliably assessed using the available evaluation datasets. Video-Frame Similarity Some images originate from nearby video frames. Although original-filename overlaps were removed, visually similar frames may still occur across dataset splits. Consequently, filename-based separation does not guarantee complete statistical independence. Annotation Quality Geometric validation cannot establish whether the defect categories or bounding-box locations are visually correct. Further manual annotation review would improve confidence in the dataset. 8. Reproducibility Dataset exploration and preparation are implemented in: notebooks/01_dataset_exploration.ipynb notebooks/02_dataset_preparation.ipynb COCO-to-YOLO conversion is implemented in: notebooks/04_yolo_model.ipynb The original and processed image datasets are excluded from Git version control.

docs.text: Evaluation and Results 1. Overview This project evaluates two approaches to automated pork packaging defect detection: HOG + SVM sliding-window detection. YOLO11n deep-learning object detection. Evaluation considers detection accuracy, computational performance and generalisation to unseen images. The experiments include: HOG + SVM baseline evaluation. Initial and extended YOLO validation. Comparison of detection performance. Inference time and GPU memory benchmarking. Final evaluation on the held-out test dataset. 2. Evaluation Dataset The processed dataset contains the following splits: Split Images Annotations Training 1,741 2,201 Validation 114 144 Testing 76 93 The validation dataset was used for model development and performance comparison. The test dataset was reserved for the final assessment of the selected YOLO model. 3. Evaluation Metrics 3.1 True and False Detections Detections were evaluated by matching predicted bounding boxes to ground-truth annotations. For the custom model comparison, an IoU threshold of 0.50 was used. Each ground-truth box could be matched to only one prediction. The resulting counts were: True Positive (TP): Correctly localised defect. False Positive (FP): Unmatched predicted defect. False Negative (FN): Missed annotated defect. 3.2 Precision Precision measures the proportion of predictions that correspond to ground-truth objects. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) 3.3 Recall Recall measures the proportion of ground-truth objects successfully detected. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) 3.4 F1-score The F1-score combines precision and recall. F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall) 3.5 Mean Average Precision YOLO performance was also evaluated using: mAP@0.5: Mean average precision at IoU 0.50. mAP@0.5:0.95: Mean average precision averaged across IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95. These metrics assess object detection across confidence thresholds and, for mAP@0.5:0.95, multiple localisation requirements. 4. HOG + SVM Baseline Results The traditional baseline used HOG features with a linear Support Vector Machine. Defects were detected using multiscale sliding windows and non-maximum suppression. 4.1 Full-Image Detection Results The baseline was evaluated on 114 validation images containing 144 annotated defects. Metric Result True Positives 1 False Positives 832 False Negatives 143 Precision 0.12% Recall 0.69% F1-score 0.20% Mean processing time 4,362.98 ms/image 4.2 Interpretation The baseline achieved very limited full-image detection performance. Only one annotated defect was successfully matched at IoU 0.50. The large number of false positives indicates that many background regions were incorrectly identified as defects. The low recall shows that most annotated defects were not detected. Although the SVM achieved approximately 85% classification accuracy during cropped-region evaluation, this did not translate into effective full-image object detection. This distinction illustrates the additional difficulty of defect localisation compared with classifying predefined image regions. 5. YOLO Validation Results 5.1 Initial and Extended Models Metric Initial YOLO Extended YOLO Precision 64.63% 84.40% Recall 55.59% 59.74% mAP@0.5 60.29% 72.13% mAP@0.5:0.95 29.14% 34.00% 5.2 Improvements After Extended Training Metric Improvement Precision +19.77 percentage points Recall +4.15 percentage points mAP@0.5 +11.84 percentage points mAP@0.5:0.95 +4.86 percentage points Extended training improved all four reported validation metrics. The largest increase was observed in precision. The increase in mAP@0.5 indicates improved overall detection performance. However, mAP@0.5:0.95 remained relatively low, suggesting that accurate bounding-box localisation continued to be challenging. 6. HOG + SVM Versus YOLO A custom evaluation procedure was developed to compare both approaches using identical validation images. The comparison used: One-to-one bounding-box matching. An IoU threshold of 0.50. Model-specific detection thresholds. Class-agnostic matching. The HOG + SVM baseline produced very low precision and recall during full-image detection. In contrast, YOLO achieved substantially stronger validation detection performance. However, the reported Ultralytics validation metrics and custom matching metrics are calculated differently. Therefore, results from these separate evaluation procedures should not be treated as directly interchangeable. The custom comparison implemented in 04_yolo_model.ipynb provides the more consistent basis for direct comparison at fixed detection thresholds. 7. Final YOLO Test Results The extended YOLO model was evaluated on the held-out test dataset. The dataset contained 76 images and 93 annotated defects. Metric Test Result Precision 47.44% Recall 51.64% mAP@0.5 55.80% mAP@0.5:0.95 25.50% 7.1 Interpretation The extended model successfully detected some defects in previously unseen images. However, test performance was lower than the reported validation performance. This indicates that the validation results did not fully represent model performance on the held-out test dataset. Possible contributing factors include: Limited dataset size. Unequal class representation. Differences in image conditions. Similarity among training images. Difficulty distinguishing subtle defects. These explanations are plausible limitations rather than individually verified causes of the performance reduction. 7.2 Generalisation Gap Metric Validation Test Precision 84.40% 47.44% Recall 59.74% 51.64% mAP@0.5 72.13% 55.80% mAP@0.5:0.95 34.00% 25.50% The decrease in test performance demonstrates the importance of evaluating detection models on held-out data. The available results are insufficient to establish reliable performance under different industrial operating conditions. 8. Computational Performance 8.1 Inference Benchmarking The initial and extended YOLO models were benchmarked using identical test images. The benchmarking procedure measured: Mean time per image. Standard deviation of processing time. Throughput in frames per second. Peak allocated GPU memory. Both models used: Parameter Value Image resolution 640 Confidence threshold 0.30 Batch size 4 GPU device 0 GPU synchronisation was used to improve timing accuracy. 8.2 Repeated Benchmarking Additional benchmarking was conducted over three rounds. Model evaluation order was alternated between rounds to reduce ordering effects. Each round used two internal timing repetitions per model. The recorded results were exported to: results/yolo_runtime_repeated.csv Average runtime and throughput were calculated to examine performance consistency. 8.3 Interpretation The lightweight YOLO11n architecture supports efficient GPU-based inference. However, computational comparisons must account for hardware differences. The traditional baseline was evaluated on the CPU, whereas YOLO was evaluated on an NVIDIA GPU. Consequently, the timing results describe the implemented systems rather than a controlled comparison on identical hardware. Measured processing time also includes model preprocessing and postprocessing. 9. Qualitative Evaluation Ground-truth annotations were visually compared with model predictions. The qualitative analysis considered: Correctly detected defects. Missed annotated defects. False-positive detections. Bounding-box localisation quality. Differences across defect categories. These comparisons help identify failure modes that may not be obvious from aggregate numerical metrics. 10. Limitations 10.1 Dataset Imbalance The five defect categories are not equally represented. The wrinkle category has no annotated examples in the validation or test sets. Its detection performance therefore cannot be assessed reliably using these evaluation splits. 10.2 Detection Thresholds Precision and recall depend on the confidence or decision threshold. A threshold suitable for one application may not be appropriate for another. 10.3 Class-Agnostic Comparison The custom HOG + SVM versus YOLO comparison evaluates bounding-box localisation without requiring correct class identification. It does not measure multiclass classification performance. 10.4 Hardware Differences CPU and GPU runtime measurements should not be interpreted as equal-hardware performance. 10.5 Limited Test Coverage The held-out test dataset contains 76 images. A larger and more diverse test dataset would provide stronger evidence of generalisation. 11. Overall Findings The experiments show that: HOG + SVM performed poorly when applied to full-image defect detection. YOLO11n achieved substantially better detection performance during validation. Extended training improved the reported YOLO validation metrics. Performance decreased on the held-out test dataset. Additional data and model refinement are necessary before considering real-world deployment. The results demonstrate the potential of deep-learning object detection for packaging inspection while identifying important limitations in robustness and generalisation. 12. Supporting Implementation Evaluation procedures and figures are implemented in: notebooks/03_baseline_model.ipynb notebooks/04_yolo_model.ipynb Additional runtime measurements are stored in the results/ directory.

docs.text: Computational Methodology 1. Overview This project investigates automated pork packaging defect detection using two computer vision approaches: Traditional machine learning using Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) and Support Vector Machine (SVM). Deep learning using YOLO11n object detection. Both approaches were evaluated using bounding-box detection metrics to compare their effectiveness. 2. Traditional Machine Learning: HOG + SVM 2.1 Image Preprocessing Input images are processed using OpenCV. Candidate image regions are converted to grayscale and resized to 64 × 64 pixels before HOG feature extraction. Consistent preprocessing is required during both model training and inference. 2.2 HOG Feature Extraction Histogram of Oriented Gradients describes local edge orientations and image texture. The following parameters were used: Parameter Value Input size 64 × 64 pixels Orientations 9 Pixels per cell 8 × 8 Cells per block 2 × 2 Block normalisation L2-Hys Each image region is represented by a 1,764-element feature vector. 2.3 SVM Classification A linear Support Vector Machine was trained to distinguish defect regions from background regions. The classification pipeline included feature standardisation using StandardScaler. Parameter Value Classifier LinearSVC C 1.0 Class weighting Balanced Maximum iterations 10,000 Random seed 42 2.4 Sliding-Window Detection For full-image detection, candidate regions are generated using a multiscale sliding-window approach. Parameter Value Base window size 128 × 128 pixels Scale factors 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 Stride 64 pixels SVM decision threshold 4.0 NMS IoU threshold 0.3 Each candidate region is converted into HOG features and classified using the trained SVM. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping predictions. The method can be computationally expensive because many candidate regions must be evaluated individually. 3. Deep Learning: YOLO11n 3.1 Model Selection YOLO11n was selected as a lightweight object-detection architecture. Unlike the sliding-window baseline, YOLO predicts object locations and classes directly from an input image. The pretrained yolo11n.pt checkpoint was used for transfer learning. 3.2 Dataset Format YOLO requires images and corresponding normalised bounding-box annotations. The processed COCO dataset was converted into YOLO format with five defect classes. The dataset configuration is stored in: data/yolo/dataset.yaml 3.3 Initial Training The initial model was trained using the following settings: Parameter Value Model YOLO11n Epochs 20 Image resolution 640 Batch size 4 Device CUDA GPU Random seed 42 Training was performed using the Ultralytics framework. 3.4 Extended Training An additional training experiment was performed using the best checkpoint from the initial training run. The extended experiment used another 20 training epochs to investigate whether additional optimisation improved detection performance. The best checkpoint from the extended experiment was used for subsequent evaluation. 4. Detection Postprocessing 4.1 Confidence Thresholding YOLO predictions are filtered using a confidence threshold. A confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis was conducted to investigate changes in precision and recall. A confidence threshold of 0.30 was used for the subsequent custom model comparison. 4.2 Non-Maximum Suppression Non-maximum suppression removes redundant overlapping predictions. Its IoU threshold is distinct from the IoU threshold used to determine whether a prediction matches a ground-truth box. 5. Evaluation Methodology 5.1 Intersection over Union Intersection over Union (IoU) measures the overlap between a predicted bounding box and its ground-truth box. IoU = Intersection Area / Union Area A prediction is considered correctly localised when its IoU meets the evaluation threshold. 5.2 Detection Metrics The following metrics are used: Precision Precision = TP / (TP + FP) Recall Recall = TP / (TP + FN) F1-score F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall) Where: TP: True positives FP: False positives FN: False negatives YOLO is also evaluated using mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95. 5.3 Baseline-versus-YOLO Comparison Both detectors are compared on the same validation images. Predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes are matched using an IoU threshold of 0.50. Each ground-truth box can be matched to a maximum of one prediction. This custom comparison is class-agnostic and evaluates defect localisation rather than class identification. The comparison uses each model's specified detection threshold, so the results represent performance at those operating points. 6. Computational Performance Inference time was measured using Python's time.perf_counter() . For GPU inference, CUDA synchronisation was performed before and after timing to account for asynchronous GPU operations. The following computational metrics were collected: Mean processing time per image Standard deviation of processing time Throughput in frames per second Peak PyTorch GPU memory allocation Repeated benchmarking was performed with alternating model evaluation order to reduce measurement-order bias. 7. Methodological Limitations HOG + SVM Detection depends on predefined window sizes and strides. Feature extraction is computationally expensive. The model does not directly predict defect categories. Performance depends on feature extraction and thresholding. YOLO11n Detection performance depends on the quality and representativeness of training annotations. Underrepresented classes may be detected less reliably. Confidence thresholds affect precision and recall. GPU performance depends on the available hardware. Comparison Limitations HOG + SVM inference was performed on the CPU, while YOLO inference was performed on a CUDA GPU. Therefore, runtime measurements compare the implemented systems rather than identical hardware configurations. The class-agnostic comparison also does not establish whether YOLO correctly identifies each defect category. 8. Implementation The computational methods are implemented in: notebooks/03_baseline_model.ipynb notebooks/04_yolo_model.ipynb The notebooks provide training code, experimental parameters, evaluation procedures and visualisations.

The following parameters were used: Parameter Value Input size 64 × 64 pixels Orientations 9 Pixels per cell 8 × 8 Cells per block 2 × 2 Block normalisation L2-Hys Each image region is represented by a 1,764-element feature vector.
docs.title: 2.2 HOG Feature Extraction

docs.text: A linear Support Vector Machine was trained to distinguish defect regions from background regions. The classification pipeline included feature standardisation using StandardScaler. Parameter Value Classifier LinearSVC C 1.0 Class weighting Balanced Maximum iterations 10,000 Random seed 42
docs.title: 2.3 SVM Classification

docs.text: For full-image detection, candidate regions are generated using a multiscale sliding-window approach. Parameter Value Base window size 128 × 128 pixels Scale factors 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 Stride 64 pixels SVM decision threshold 4.0 NMS IoU threshold 0.3 Each candidate region is converted into HOG features and classified using the trained SVM. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping predictions. The method can be computationally expensive because many candidate regions must be evaluated individually.
docs.title: 2.4 Sliding-Window Detection

docs.text: YOLO11n was selected as a lightweight object-detection architecture. Unlike the sliding-window baseline, YOLO predicts object locations and classes directly from an input image. The pretrained yolo11n.pt checkpoint was used for transfer learning.
docs.title: 3.1 Model Selection

docs.text: YOLO requires images and corresponding normalised bounding-box annotations. The processed COCO dataset was converted into YOLO format with five defect classes. The dataset configuration is stored in: data/yolo/dataset.yaml
docs.title: 3.2 Dataset Format

docs.text: The initial model was trained using the following settings: Parameter Value Model YOLO11n Epochs 20 Image resolution 640 Batch size 4 Device CUDA GPU Random seed 42 Training was performed using the Ultralytics framework.
docs.title: 3.3 Initial Training

docs.text: An additional training experiment was performed using the best checkpoint from the initial training run. The extended experiment used another 20 training epochs to investigate whether additional optimisation improved detection performance. The best checkpoint from the extended experiment was used for subsequent evaluation.
docs.title: 3.4 Extended Training

docs.text: YOLO predictions are filtered using a confidence threshold. A confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis was conducted to investigate changes in precision and recall. A confidence threshold of 0.30 was used for the subsequent custom model comparison.
docs.title: 4.1 Confidence Thresholding

docs.text: Non-maximum suppression removes redundant overlapping predictions. Its IoU threshold is distinct from the IoU threshold used to determine whether a prediction matches a ground-truth box.
docs.title: 4.2 Non-Maximum Suppression

docs.text: Intersection over Union (IoU) measures the overlap between a predicted bounding box and its ground-truth box. IoU = Intersection Area / Union Area A prediction is considered correctly localised when its IoU meets the evaluation threshold.
docs.title: 5.1 Intersection over Union

docs.text: The following metrics are used: Precision Precision = TP / (TP + FP) Recall Recall = TP / (TP + FN) F1-score F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall) Where: TP: True positives FP: False positives FN: False negatives YOLO is also evaluated using mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95.
docs.title: 5.2 Detection Metrics

docs.text: Both detectors are compared on the same validation images. Predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes are matched using an IoU threshold of 0.50. Each ground-truth box can be matched to a maximum of one prediction. This custom comparison is class-agnostic and evaluates defect localisation rather than class identification. The comparison uses each model's specified detection threshold, so the results represent performance at those operating points.
docs.title: 5.3 Baseline-versus-YOLO Comparison

docs.text: Inference time was measured using Python's time.perf_counter() . For GPU inference, CUDA synchronisation was performed before and after timing to account for asynchronous GPU operations. The following computational metrics were collected: Mean processing time per image Standard deviation of processing time Throughput in frames per second Peak PyTorch GPU memory allocation Repeated benchmarking was performed with alternating model evaluation order to reduce measurement-order bias.
docs.title: 6. Computational Performance

docs.text: Detection depends on predefined window sizes and strides. Feature extraction is computationally expensive. The model does not directly predict defect categories. Performance depends on feature extraction and thresholding.
docs.title: HOG + SVM

docs.text: Detection performance depends on the quality and representativeness of training annotations. Underrepresented classes may be detected less reliably. Confidence thresholds affect precision and recall. GPU performance depends on the available hardware.
docs.title: YOLO11n

docs.text: HOG + SVM inference was performed on the CPU, while YOLO inference was performed on a CUDA GPU. Therefore, runtime measurements compare the implemented systems rather than identical hardware configurations. The class-agnostic comparison also does not establish whether YOLO correctly identifies each defect category.

docs.title: 8. Implementation

docs.text: Model Training and Optimisation 1. Overview This project developed a YOLO11n object detector to identify five categories of pork packaging and visual meat defects. The training process consisted of two experiments: Initial training using pretrained YOLO11n weights. Extended training using the best checkpoint from the initial experiment. The objective was to evaluate whether additional training improved detection performance. 2. Training Environment Model training was performed using Python and the Ultralytics YOLO framework. Component Configuration Python 3.11.9 Model architecture YOLO11n Deep learning framework PyTorch Training library Ultralytics GPU NVIDIA RTX 4050 Laptop GPU GPU memory 6 GB Acceleration CUDA Random seed 42 The GPU was used to accelerate training and inference. The recorded software versions and dependencies are documented in the project's requirements file. 3. Training Dataset The model was trained using the processed dataset following duplicate-filename checks. Split Images Annotations Training 1,741 2,201 Validation 114 144 Testing 76 93 The training dataset was used for parameter optimisation. The validation dataset was used to assess performance during model development. The test dataset was reserved for final evaluation. All images and labels were organised in the directory: data/yolo/ The dataset configuration was defined in: data/yolo/dataset.yaml 4. Initial YOLO Training 4.1 Model Initialisation The initial experiment used the pretrained checkpoint: yolo11n.pt Pretrained weights provided a starting point for fine-tuning the detector on the pork packaging dataset. 4.2 Training Configuration Parameter Value Epochs 20 Image resolution 640 × 640 Batch size 4 GPU device 0 Data-loader workers 0 Random seed 42 Training run initial_training Training outputs, including model checkpoints and performance figures, were saved by Ultralytics. The best checkpoint was stored as best.pt within the experiment's weights directory. 4.3 Initial Validation Results Metric Initial YOLO Precision 64.63% Recall 55.59% mAP@0.5 60.29% mAP@0.5:0.95 29.14% The initial model demonstrated the ability to detect packaging-related defects. However, recall and bounding-box localisation accuracy indicated potential for further improvement. 5. Extended YOLO Training 5.1 Training Approach The extended experiment was initialised using the best checkpoint from the initial experiment. An additional 20 training epochs were performed using the same processed dataset. This continued optimisation from previously learned model parameters rather than starting again from the original pretrained checkpoint. 5.2 Extended Training Configuration Parameter Value Starting weights Initial best.pt Additional epochs 20 Image resolution 640 × 640 Batch size 4 GPU device 0 Data-loader workers 0 Random seed 42 Training run extended_training The best checkpoint from this experiment was selected as the final model for subsequent evaluation. 6. Validation Performance Comparison Metric Initial YOLO Extended YOLO Improvement Precision 64.63% 84.40% +19.77 pp Recall 55.59% 59.74% +4.15 pp mAP@0.5 60.29% 72.13% +11.84 pp mAP@0.5:0.95 29.14% 34.00% +4.86 pp pp = percentage points. Extended training improved all four reported validation metrics. The largest improvement was observed in precision, which increased by 19.77 percentage points. The mAP@0.5 improvement indicates better detection performance across confidence thresholds. The improvement in mAP@0.5:0.95 was smaller, suggesting that accurate bounding-box localisation remained challenging. These results supported selecting the extended YOLO checkpoint for further evaluation. 7. Confidence-Threshold Sensitivity The extended model was evaluated using several confidence thresholds. Confidence Precision Recall 0.10 84.40% 59.74% 0.20 84.40% 59.74% 0.30 83.20% 60.18% 0.40 93.47% 51.46% 0.50 90.04% 29.40% 0.60 74.29% 16.48% 7.1 Interpretation The results demonstrate the effect of confidence threshold selection on detection performance. A threshold of 0.30 produced the highest observed recall among the tested values. A threshold of 0.40 produced the highest observed precision. Higher thresholds generally reduced the number of retained detections, although precision did not increase monotonically. 7.2 Selected Operating Threshold A confidence threshold of 0.30 was selected for the custom comparison with the HOG + SVM baseline. This threshold provides a useful operating point for examining the balance between correctly detected defects and missed defects. The selected threshold does not necessarily represent an optimal industrial operating point. 7.3 Evaluation Considerations The confidence-threshold experiment used an NMS IoU threshold of 0.70. This is separate from the IoU thresholds used to calculate object-detection evaluation metrics. The mAP values produced under different confidence cutoffs should not be interpreted as directly comparable standard full-confidence-range AP values. 8. Model Selection The extended YOLO11n checkpoint was selected for final evaluation because it achieved better validation performance than the initial model. The final model was then evaluated on the held-out test dataset. The test results are reported separately in the Evaluation and Results documentation. This separation is important because validation performance may not accurately represent performance on previously unseen images. 9. Training Limitations Class Imbalance Some defect classes contain substantially fewer training examples than others. This can affect the model's ability to learn reliable features for underrepresented categories. Missing Evaluation Classes The wrinkle category has no annotations in the validation or test datasets. Consequently, its detection performance cannot be reliably established from these evaluation splits. Limited Dataset Diversity Images from similar capture conditions may share visual characteristics. The trained model may therefore perform less reliably on substantially different packaging, lighting or camera conditions. Limited Hyperparameter Exploration The project investigated additional training and confidence-threshold sensitivity. It did not perform an exhaustive search across architectures or training hyperparameters. 10. Reproducibility The training and optimisation experiments are implemented in: notebooks/04_yolo_model.ipynb The notebook includes: YOLO dataset conversion and validation. Initial model training. Extended model training. Validation metric extraction. Confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis. Runtime and GPU memory benchmarking. Final model evaluation. Training checkpoints and large datasets may need to be obtained or regenerated separately if they are excluded from the GitHub repository.

docs.title: 10. Reproducibility

docs.text: Reproducibility 1. Overview This section describes the software environment, project structure and execution procedure used to develop and evaluate the pork packaging defect detection system. The project implements two approaches: HOG + SVM traditional machine-learning baseline. YOLO11n deep-learning object detector. The experiments are organised into four Jupyter notebooks. Reproducing the results requires access to the original dataset, the project source code and compatible Python dependencies. 2. Software Environment The original development environment used: Component Configuration Operating system Windows Python 3.11.9 Development environment Visual Studio Code Notebook environment Jupyter Deep learning framework PyTorch Object detection framework Ultralytics Image processing OpenCV, scikit-image Machine learning scikit-learn Data analysis NumPy, pandas Visualisation Matplotlib GPU NVIDIA RTX 4050 Laptop GPU GPU memory 6 GB The project dependencies are recorded in requirements.txt . Exact software versions and hardware configurations may affect computational performance and numerical reproducibility. 3. Project Structure The main project directories are organised as follows: MMA3001-Pork-Packaging-Inspection/ | |-- data/ | |-- processed/ | |-- yolo/ | |-- docs/ | |-- index.md | |-- dataset.md | |-- methodology.md | |-- model_training.md | |-- evaluation.md | |-- reproducibility.md | |-- models/ | |-- notebooks/ | |-- 01_dataset_exploration.ipynb | |-- 02_dataset_preparation.ipynb | |-- 03_baseline_model.ipynb | |-- 04_yolo_model.ipynb | |-- results/ | |-- mkdocs.yml |-- requirements.txt |-- README.md Large datasets and trained model checkpoints may be excluded from Git version control. Some output directories are generated automatically when the corresponding notebooks are executed. 4. Installation 4.1 Clone the Repository Clone the project from its GitHub repository. git clone <repository-url> Replace <repository-url> with the actual repository URL. Navigate to the project directory: cd MMA3001-Pork-Packaging-Inspection 4.2 Create a Virtual Environment For Windows PowerShell: python -m venv .venv Activate the virtual environment: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 If PowerShell blocks activation, the environment can still be used by calling the Python executable directly. 4.3 Install Dependencies Install the required packages: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt The original experiments used a CUDA-enabled PyTorch installation. Users intending to reproduce GPU training should verify that PyTorch recognises their NVIDIA GPU. 4.4 Verify GPU Availability Run the following Python code: import torch print(torch.__version__) print(torch.cuda.is_available()) A CUDA-compatible environment should report True for GPU availability. CPU-only environments may require changes to the YOLO device settings. 5. Dataset Requirements The original image dataset is required to reproduce dataset preparation and model training. The dataset must contain COCO-format annotation files and the corresponding images. The processed dataset uses three splits: Split Images Annotations Training 1,741 2,201 Validation 114 144 Testing 76 93 The dataset preparation notebook produces the processed annotations and split assignments. The YOLO notebook converts these annotations into the required YOLO format. The YOLO dataset configuration is stored at: data/yolo/dataset.yaml The original dataset is not automatically downloaded by the project notebooks. 6. Notebook Execution Order The notebooks should be executed in numerical order. Notebook 01 — Dataset Exploration File: notebooks/01_dataset_exploration.ipynb Purpose: Inspect the dataset structure. Calculate image and annotation counts. Examine defect class distributions. Visualise annotated images. Investigate duplicated source filenames. Identify potential data-quality issues. Notebook 02 — Dataset Preparation File: notebooks/02_dataset_preparation.ipynb Purpose: Group images by original filename. Assign original-image groups to dataset splits. Remove cross-split filename overlap. Prepare cleaned COCO annotations. Validate image references and bounding boxes. Save the processed dataset. This notebook modifies generated dataset files. Review its file operations before rerunning it on an existing processed dataset. Notebook 03 — HOG + SVM Baseline File: notebooks/03_baseline_model.ipynb Purpose: Prepare positive and negative training samples. Extract HOG features. Train a linear SVM classifier. Evaluate cropped-region classification. Implement multiscale sliding-window detection. Apply non-maximum suppression. Evaluate full-image defect detection. The trained SVM is saved as: models/hog_svm_baseline.joblib Notebook 04 — YOLO Model File: notebooks/04_yolo_model.ipynb Purpose: Convert COCO annotations into YOLO labels. Validate the converted dataset. Train the initial YOLO11n model. Continue training from the initial checkpoint. Compare validation performance. Analyse confidence thresholds. Benchmark runtime and GPU memory usage. Compare HOG + SVM and YOLO detection. Evaluate the selected model on test images. The notebook uses checkpoints generated by the training experiments. 7. Random Seeds A random seed of 42 was used in the model development experiments. Random seeds were applied where supported to reduce variation between experimental runs. However, identical seeds do not guarantee perfectly identical results. Differences may arise from: GPU hardware. CUDA and PyTorch versions. Parallel processing. Nondeterministic operations. Dependency versions. Reproduced results should therefore be compared within a reasonable numerical tolerance. 8. Model Checkpoints The HOG + SVM baseline is stored as a serialised scikit-learn model. The YOLO experiments generate trained PyTorch checkpoint files. The relevant YOLO checkpoints are: Initial training: best.pt . Extended training: best.pt . The extended model uses the best checkpoint from the initial experiment as its starting point. Model checkpoint paths are established by the training runs in Notebook 04. If checkpoint files are unavailable, the training experiments must be rerun. Only load serialised models from trusted sources. 9. Evaluation Reproduction 9.1 HOG + SVM The traditional baseline is evaluated on validation images using: Sliding-window candidate regions. SVM decision threshold of 4.0. Non-maximum suppression at IoU 0.30. Detection matching at IoU 0.50. 9.2 YOLO The extended YOLO model is evaluated using the Ultralytics validation procedure. The reported metrics include: Precision. Recall. mAP@0.5. mAP@0.5:0.95. A confidence threshold of 0.30 is used for the custom baseline-versus-YOLO comparison. 9.3 Detection Comparison Both models are evaluated on the same validation images. Predictions are matched to ground-truth annotations using class-agnostic, one-to-one bounding-box matching. The resulting true-positive, false-positive and false-negative counts are used to calculate precision, recall and F1-score. This custom comparison is distinct from Ultralytics' class-aware mAP evaluation. 10. Computational Benchmarking YOLO inference benchmarks use: Parameter Value Image resolution 640 Confidence threshold 0.30 Batch size 4 GPU device 0 GPU synchronisation is used before and after timed inference operations. The benchmark records: Mean processing time per image. Standard deviation of processing time. Throughput in frames per second. Peak allocated GPU memory. Repeated measurements alternate model execution order to reduce timing bias. The recorded benchmark results are saved in: results/yolo_runtime_repeated.csv Runtime results depend on the hardware and software environment. 11. Expected Results 11.1 Extended YOLO Validation Metric Result Precision 84.40% Recall 59.74% mAP@0.5 72.13% mAP@0.5:0.95 34.00% 11.2 Final YOLO Test Evaluation Metric Result Precision 47.44% Recall 51.64% mAP@0.5 55.80% mAP@0.5:0.95 25.50% These values are reference results from the original experiments. Minor numerical differences may occur when reproducing model training. 12. Known Limitations Reproducibility is subject to several constraints. Dataset Availability The original images and annotations must be obtained separately if they are not included in the repository. GPU Requirements The original YOLO experiments used CUDA GPU acceleration. Different hardware may produce different training times and results. Class Representation The dataset contains uneven numbers of examples across defect categories. The wrinkle category is absent from the validation and test annotations. Model Generalisation The extended model achieved lower performance on the held-out test dataset than on the validation dataset. Consequently, the reported results should not be interpreted as proof of reliable industrial performance. Data Independence Original-filename grouping prevents identical source filenames from crossing dataset splits. It does not guarantee that visually similar video frames are independent. 13. Documentation Build The project documentation is generated using MkDocs. Install the documentation tool: python -m pip install mkdocs Preview the website locally: python -m mkdocs serve Open the local address: http://127.0.0.1:8000/ Generate the static HTML website: python -m mkdocs build The HTML output is generated inside the site/ directory. To check for documentation warnings: python -m mkdocs build --strict 14. Reproducibility Checklist Before reproducing the experiments, verify that: [ ] The original dataset is available. [ ] The Python environment is configured. [ ] Required dependencies are installed. [ ] The notebooks use the correct project paths. [ ] Dataset preparation completes successfully. [ ] COCO-to-YOLO conversion passes validation. [ ] The HOG + SVM classifier can be trained or loaded. [ ] YOLO checkpoint paths are available. [ ] Evaluation uses the documented thresholds. [ ] Results are compared against reference metrics. [ ] The MkDocs website builds without warnings. 15. Conclusion The project provides a structured computational workflow for automated pork packaging defect detection. The notebooks document dataset preparation, traditional machine-learning development, deep-learning model training and evaluation. Combined with the documented environment and experimental settings, these materials support independent inspection and reproduction of the computational methodology.

docs.text: The traditional baseline is evaluated on validation images using: Sliding-window candidate regions. SVM decision threshold of 4.0. Non-maximum suppression at IoU 0.30. Detection matching at IoU 0.50.
docs.title: 9.1 HOG + SVM

docs.text: The extended YOLO model is evaluated using the Ultralytics validation procedure. The reported metrics include: Precision. Recall. mAP@0.5. mAP@0.5:0.95. A confidence threshold of 0.30 is used for the custom baseline-versus-YOLO comparison.
docs.title: 9.2 YOLO

docs.text: Both models are evaluated on the same validation images. Predictions are matched to ground-truth annotations using class-agnostic, one-to-one bounding-box matching. The resulting true-positive, false-positive and false-negative counts are used to calculate precision, recall and F1-score. This custom comparison is distinct from Ultralytics' class-aware mAP evaluation.
docs.title: 9.3 Detection Comparison

docs.text: YOLO inference benchmarks use: Parameter Value Image resolution 640 Confidence threshold 0.30 Batch size 4 GPU device 0 GPU synchronisation is used before and after timed inference operations. The benchmark records: Mean processing time per image. Standard deviation of processing time. Throughput in frames per second. Peak allocated GPU memory. Repeated measurements alternate model execution order to reduce timing bias. The recorded benchmark results are saved in: results/yolo_runtime_repeated.csv Runtime results depend on the hardware and software environment.

docs.title: 12. Known Limitations

docs.text: The original images and annotations must be obtained separately if they are not included in the repository.
docs.title: Dataset Availability

docs.text: The original YOLO experiments used CUDA GPU acceleration. Different hardware may produce different training times and results.
docs.title: GPU Requirements

docs.text: The dataset contains uneven numbers of examples across defect categories. The wrinkle category is absent from the validation and test annotations.
docs.title: Class Representation

docs.text: The extended model achieved lower performance on the held-out test dataset than on the validation dataset. Consequently, the reported results should not be interpreted as proof of reliable industrial performance.
docs.title: Model Generalisation

docs.text: Original-filename grouping prevents identical source filenames from crossing dataset splits. It does not guarantee that visually similar video frames are independent.

docs.title: 14. Reproducibility Checklist

docs.text: The project provides a structured computational workflow for automated pork packaging defect detection. The notebooks document dataset preparation, traditional machine-learning development, deep-learning model training and evaluation. Combined with the documented environment and experimental settings, these materials support independent inspection and reproduction of the computational methodology.
